development-of-practical-skills: Plants given a new fertiliser grew taller, but they also sat nearest the window. Can you trust the result?
Five readings agree perfectly. How can every one of them still be wrong?
Two sets of results share the same average but look nothing alike. What number captures the difference?
Two bars on a graph have different heights. When does that difference actually mean something?
A difference between two groups could be real or just luck. How do biologists decide which?
Leaves in the shade look bigger than leaves in the sun. How big must the gap be before you believe it?
Why does warming an enzyme speed it up, until suddenly it hardly works at all?
foundations-in-biology: An electron microscope shows a cell packed with odd shapes. How do you tell what each one is and does?
A plant cell shares most of its parts with yours. So what does it have that yours lacks, and why?
Your pancreas makes enzymes that digest protein. How does it ship them out without digesting itself?
A bacterium has no nucleus. So where does it keep its genes, and what else does it manage without?
exchange-transport: Why can an amoeba survive without lungs or a heart, but you can't?
What do lungs, gills and leaves have in common that makes them so good at swapping gases?
How do your lungs pull air in when they have no muscle of their own?
How can you tell from the outside how well a person's lungs are working?
How do fish and insects get oxygen to their cells without lungs?
biodiversity-evolution-disease: Your body carries trillions of microbes, yet very few make you ill. What makes something a pathogen?
A plant cannot run away or make antibodies. So how does it stop an infection from spreading?
Most germs that land on you never get in, and most that do never get far. What stops them?
Blood must flow freely through every vessel, yet seal a cut within minutes. How does it do both?
Your body has never met this year's flu virus, yet it makes antibodies that fit it. How?
A second infection with the same virus often passes without you noticing. What changed inside you?
communication-homeostasis-energy: A hormone in your blood reaches almost every cell, yet only a few respond. How do cells pick their messages?
Your body temperature wobbles all day. Why is that a sign that control is working, not failing?
Your core temperature barely moves in snow or in sun. How does your body manage that, and at what cost?
genetics-evolution-ecosystems: Change one letter in a gene: does the protein always change?
Nearly every cell in your body carries the same genes. So why doesn't a skin cell act like a nerve cell?
Bacteria make the enzymes for milk sugar only when it is there. How do they know when to start?
A gene has already been copied into a message. Can the cell still stop its protein being made?
An early embryo is a ball of identical cells. How does it know where to build a head and a tail?
biological-membranes: A cell's outer membrane is just two molecules thick. Why do its molecules form that sheet by themselves?
How can you show that the molecules in a membrane never stop moving?
Oxygen slips straight through a cell membrane, yet a smaller sodium ion is stopped. Why?
Why are the cells lining the small intestine covered in thousands of tiny finger-like folds?
biological-membranes-part-2: A cell keeps taking in a substance it already holds more of than its surroundings. How is that possible?
Why are almost all cells too small to see, even inside the largest animals?
Why would a drip of pure water into a patient's vein do harm?
Potato pieces gain mass in some sugar solutions and lose it in others. What does the point in between reveal?
biological-molecules: Why does salt vanish into water while oil sits on top in a separate layer?
How can weak attractions between molecules hold up an insect and keep a lake's temperature steady?
Every time your cells build a big molecule, they make water. Why?
Glucose and fructose are built from exactly the same atoms. So what makes them different sugars?
Starch and cellulose are both chains of glucose. Why can one feed you while the other builds a tree?
Why is butter solid but olive oil runny, when both are made of the same kind of molecule?
biological-molecules-part-2: Oily molecules avoid water, yet they wrap every cell in a thin film. How does that film build itself?
Every protein in your body is built from just twenty building blocks. How can so few make so many?
A protein is only a chain of amino acids. So how does it fold into the exact shape its job needs?
A tendon protein is tough as rope, a blood protein dissolves. Both are amino acid chains. Why so different?
Why can a shortage of one simple charged particle stop a cell, or a whole plant, from working properly?
cell-division-and-organisation: Your body makes about four million new cells a second. How does each one get a full set of chromosomes?
A microscope slide freezes a root tip in one instant. How can counting its cells reveal time?
Many cells in your body could still divide, yet most of the time they hold back. What keeps them in check?
Each parent passes on chromosomes, yet the number never doubles. How is it halved so exactly?
Brothers and sisters share both parents, yet each gets a different genetic mix. Where does it come from?
cell-division-and-organisation-part-2: Your nerve cells and muscle cells carry the same genes. So why are they so different?
Some of your cells have no nucleus and some have hundreds. How does a cell's build match its job?
One early embryo cell can grow into a whole baby. Why can't a cell from your bone marrow?
Scientists can turn a skin cell into one that can become almost any cell. What should we use that for?
classification-and-evolution: How can just two words tell you where any living thing fits among millions?
Two animals look almost identical. How can biologists tell whether they are truly close relatives?
How can one protein from your cells show you are closer to a dog than to a chicken?
Why are some microbes that look just like bacteria placed further from them than you are from a mushroom?
How can we trust the evidence that living things have changed over time?
classification-and-evolution-part-2: Cuttings from one plant share every gene. So why don't they all grow to the same height?
If no animal can change its own genes, how can a whole population change over time?
A desert fox has enormous ears and almost never drinks. How did it end up so well suited to the desert?
Nobody designs a drug-resistant germ, so how do whole populations of them appear so quickly?
cloning-and-biotechnology: Why would a factory lock its enzymes in place when free enzymes work faster?
Can one cell from an adult animal's body be used to make a whole new animal?
How can a tank of tiny living cells make medicines, cheese and even clean up oil spills?
development-of-practical-skills-part-2: Many foods hide sugar, starch, protein or fat. How can a few drops of reagent tell you which, and how much?
One spot of a mixture goes in; a ladder of spots comes out. How do you work out what each spot is?
How does water reach the top of the tallest tree with no pump and no energy spent by the tree?
Why does a plant lose water fastest on a warm, dry, windy day, and how can you measure it?
Why does beetroot bleed its red pigment into hot water but not into cold?
How do you grow bacteria on purpose without growing anything else, or infecting yourself?
Bacteria can go from a handful to billions overnight. How do you count them, and how do you graph that?
development-of-practical-skills-part-3: How can you measure the length of a cell you can only see through a microscope?
If you can enlarge an image as much as you like, why do some things inside a cell stay blurred?
Why does a good biology drawing leave out most of what you can see down the microscope?
Cut open an organ or slice it thin: how do you know what you are looking at?
How can a speck of DNA from one hair be copied into billions and then sorted by size?
If almost all human DNA is shared, how can a trace of it point to just one person?
A plant stem can grow longer, and even bend towards a window, without making new cells. How?
development-of-practical-skills-part-4: Cut every nerve to a heart and it keeps on beating. So what are those nerves for?
How can you know how many snails live in a whole wood without finding every single one?
Two meadows hold exactly the same species. How can one of them be far more diverse than the other?
Why can a whole field of crop plants be wiped out by a single new disease?
Mendel's peas came out at almost three to one, never exactly. How close is close enough?
disease-and-the-immune-system-part-2: Some vaccines protect for life, but the flu vaccine changes every year. Why the difference?
How can a drug that once cured an infection stop working against the very same germ?
Species have always gone extinct. So why are biologists so alarmed by the extinctions happening now?
If the last of a species survives safely in a zoo, has that species really been saved?
The first human genome took years and a fortune to read. What can we do now that it is quick and cheap?
ecosystems: A rock pool and a rainforest are both called ecosystems. What do they have in common?
Energy flows along every food chain but never comes back. So where does it start, and where does it go?
A caterpillar eats a whole leaf. Why does so little of that leaf end up as caterpillar?
Why are top predators so rare, and why does eating lower in a food chain feed more people?
The carbon atoms in your body were once in the air. How do they keep being recycled?
Nearly four-fifths of the air is nitrogen. So why do crops so often run short of it?
Bare rock can turn into forest without anyone planting a single tree. How does that happen?
enzymes: How can a protein make a reaction millions of times faster, yet come out of it unchanged?
Is an enzyme a rigid lock waiting for one key, or does it change shape as its target arrives?
How can a single molecule switch off one reaction among the thousands running in a cell?
excretion: Every day your body makes enough ammonia to poison itself. Why doesn't it?
Your kidneys filter all of your blood plasma about sixty times a day. Why don't you run dry?
The kidney's filter lets sugar straight through but holds back proteins. What is it built from?
A kangaroo rat can live its whole life without drinking. How do its kidneys hold on to water?
How can a paper strip pick out one hormone from the thousands of chemicals in a urine sample?
hormonal-communication: Hormones reach almost every cell in the body. So why does each one affect only a few?
A few hormone molecules can make a cell release thousands of sugar molecules. How?
You eat a sugary snack, yet your blood sugar barely changes for long. What pulls it back?
Two people both have high blood sugar, but only one lacks insulin. How can that be?
How can a bacterium be made to produce a human hormone it has never made before?
If a goat can be made to produce a human medicine in its milk, what else could we change, and should we?
manipulating-genomes: If a gene is faulty, can we find it before birth, or even fix it?
neuronal-communication: Why does a resting nerve cell keep spending energy when it is not sending any signal?
Why do some nerve signals race faster than a car while others creep along at walking pace?
How does a gentle press on your skin, or a dim glimmer of light, become a message a nerve can carry?
A nerve signal reaches a gap it cannot jump. So how does the message get across?
One nerve cell can receive thousands of messages at once. How does it decide whether to fire?
nucleotides-and-nucleic-acids: DNA's two strands are held together only by weak bonds. So why doesn't the molecule fall apart?
DNA uses just four kinds of base. How can that be enough to hold the instructions for a whole organism?
Your cells already get energy from sugar. Why do they spend it through a different molecule first?
Before a cell divides, it copies all of its DNA. How does the copy come out almost perfect?
nucleotides-and-nucleic-acids-part-2: How did one experiment with heavy nitrogen show that every new DNA molecule keeps half of the old one?
DNA has only four letters. How can a gene spell out a protein built from twenty different building blocks?
Your DNA never leaves the nucleus. So how do its instructions reach the place where proteins are made?
A ribosome never sees a single amino acid's name. So how does it build the right protein?
patterns-of-inheritance: Two tall pea plants can produce a short one. Where was the short plant hiding?
Cross a red flower with a white one and every offspring is pink. So why do red and white come back?
If two genes sit on the same chromosome, can they ever be separated?
Why do some inherited conditions turn up far more often in sons than in daughters?
How can one gene decide whether another gene gets any say at all?
patterns-of-inheritance-part-2: Why doesn't selection always push a population in the same direction?
Why do small, isolated populations end up so genetically different from everyone else?
A harmful allele can hide in healthy carriers. How can you work out how many people carry it?
If two groups of the same animal never meet again, how do they end up as different species?
Can a new species appear right beside its parents, or even in a single generation?
photosynthesis: A plant takes in carbon dioxide and water and gives out oxygen. Which of the two did the oxygen come from?
A green leaf also hides orange and yellow pigments. How can you reveal them, and what are they for?
Burning sugar releases all its energy in one flash. How do your cells release it slowly enough to use?
A leaf splits water to get electrons. Where do those electrons end up, and what do they make on the way?
Why would a chloroplast send its electrons round in a loop that makes no oxygen at all?
Switch off the light and a leaf stops making sugar within seconds, yet that stage needs no light. Why?
Brighter lamps stop making a greenhouse crop grow any faster. What should the grower change instead?
plant-and-animal-responses: With no brain or nerves, how does a plant know when to wake a seed, open a flower or ripen its fruit?
Why does your hand jerk away from a hot pan before you have even felt the pain?
Your heart races and your pupils widen before you have decided anything. So who gave the order?
Not one filament in a contracting muscle gets shorter. So how does the whole muscle shorten?
Some muscle works all your life without tiring; some tires in seconds. What makes the difference?
populations-and-sustainability: Why does a population that doubles again and again eventually stop growing?
Why do members of the same species often compete harder with each other than with any other species?
How can losing a few otters turn a forest of seaweed into bare rock?
How can people keep taking food and materials from nature without wrecking it?
respiration: Pyruvate enters the mitochondrion with three carbon atoms. Where do they go, and what does the cell gain?
Why would a cell pump protons uphill across a membrane, only to let them flood straight back?
Mitochondria, chloroplasts and bacteria all make ATP with the same machine. What does that tell us?
When oxygen runs out, muscles make lactate and yeast makes alcohol. What do they gain from it?
How can a bead of liquid creeping along a thin tube show how fast seeds respire, and which fuel they use?
transport-in-animals: Blood leaves the heart in surges but creeps past your cells in a steady trickle. How?
Your blood vessels leak fluid all day long. So why don't your tissues flood?
Your heart has no switches, yet its valves open and close at exactly the right moments. How?
Your blood passes every tissue all day. How does it know to drop more oxygen where muscles work hardest?
transport-in-plants: How does a plant send sugar up to its buds and down to its roots at the same time?
How does water get from the soil into a root, and how do desert plants keep hold of it?
